name: Dactyl-Remnant
geological_features: Continent-spanning impact scar from ancient collision
Tectonic activity driven by residual impact energy
specific_features: Ancient impact that nearly destroyed the planet still driving geological activity
Extremophile microbial mats in hydrothermal zones
description: Dactyl-Remnant is a large barren world still recovering from an impact event that nearly destroyed it. A continent-spanning scar marks where an object roughly a quarter of the planet's own mass struck at a shallow angle approximately one billion years ago, an impact so catastrophic that it remelted a significant portion of the crust and perturbed the planet's orbit. The recrystallized impact melt sheets that cover the scar zone are some of the largest igneous formations in known space, a frozen record of the energy released in that ancient collision.

The impact's residual thermal energy continues to drive geological activity a billion years later. Hydrothermal systems along the scar zone's margins pump heated water through mineral-rich rock, creating oasis environments in an otherwise desolate landscape. The thin atmosphere is maintained partly by ongoing volcanic outgassing from these active zones, a slow replenishment that barely keeps pace with atmospheric escape to space. Without the impact's lingering heat, the atmosphere would have been lost entirely.

Extremophile microbial mats thrive in the hydrothermal zones, metabolizing sulfur and iron compounds in water heated by the ancient impact's residual energy. These organisms may be descendants of a more complex biosphere that existed before the impact, survivors that retreated to the one environment where conditions remained viable. Their biochemistry shows signs of extreme evolutionary bottleneck, consistent with a population that was nearly extinguished and rebuilt itself from a handful of surviving lineages.

The impact-concentrated platinum deposits in the scar zone are among the richest accessible deposits in the sector, the collision having gathered and concentrated metals from both the planet and the impactor into mineable formations. Large-scale extraction operations have established themselves along the scar margins, where the platinum concentrations are highest and the hydrothermal activity provides energy for processing. The microbial ecosystems are legally protected but practically vulnerable, their hydrothermal habitats overlapping uncomfortably with the most economically attractive mining zones.
